why: The narrowest key that unlocks both devices is owned by their deepest common ancestor: the lowest common ancestor in a general rooted tree. Record parent and depth with one traversal, lift the deeper node to the same depth, then lift both until they meet.
hints: A key at device d covers both targets exactly when d is an ancestor of both. Which such d has the smallest subtree?
The deepest common ancestor. With parent pointers and depths you can walk both nodes upward in step.
Iterative DFS from 0 to fill parent[] and depth[]; raise the deeper node until depths match, then step both up until equal. O(n). For many queries, binary lifting gives O(log n) each.
pitfalls: A node is its own ancestor: if p is above q, the answer is p.
Deep trees (10^5) overflow recursive DFS in Python; use a stack.
